messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 45

You’re a clinical psychologist writing psychological PTSD case vignettes. Strictly follow the instructions: third person, present tense, realistic personal narrative, not a clinical report. Tell the story chronologically from the traumatic event to the present. Show symptoms through thoughts, feelings, actions. Integrate occupation naturally. No diagnosis or treatment at the end. Length 500-700 words.

Patient: 50, male, South Eastern Asian, divorced, musician, stalking trauma, PCL-5 45.

Write the vignette.He sits on the edge of the chair, spine straight, hands resting on his thighs as if he’s about to play a chord on an invisible guitar. Fifty years old, a musician who spent three decades in the city’s busiest jazz clubs, his fingers still bear the calluses from countless nights bending notes under amber lights. His name is Tran, and he tells me his story in a voice that cracks like old varnish.

It started four years ago, after a gig at a small lounge downtown. A woman in the front row had smiled at him through the entire set, her eyes fixed. He remembers thinking she might be a fan, nothing more. The next week she was at another venue, same front row, same smile. Then the messages began—long, rambling emails about how they were destined to be together, how she could read his soul through his music. He blocked her, changed his number, but she always found him. Notes slipped under his apartment door. A voicemail at 3 a.m. playing one of his songs in a low, humming voice.

His bandmates joked about it at first. “You’ve got a groupie, man.” But the jokes stopped when she started showing up at his son’s school. Tran had joint custody then, before the divorce, and the moment he saw her standing across the street from the playground, his chest seized. He called the police. They took a report, but she was never charged—no threats, just presence. A shadow that refused to leave.

Now, sitting in my office, Tran’s eyes dart to the door every time a floorboard creaks in the hallway. He stopped playing live two years ago. His guitar case leans against the wall in his bedroom, unopened. The last time he tried to practice at home, he heard a car idling outside, and his fingers froze on the strings. He couldn’t breathe. He packed the guitar away and hasn’t touched it since.

He works part-time now, giving online lessons from his apartment, but he checks the window three times during each session. He installed extra locks, a security camera, and blackout curtains. Even so, he can’t sleep through the night. He dreams of her standing at the foot of his bed, humming that same song. He wakes in a cold sweat, heart pounding, and spends the rest of the night pacing the small living room.

His ex-wife, who left him two years after the stalking began, told him he was “never the same.” He agrees. He doesn’t go to grocery stores; he orders delivery. He avoids crowds, public transit, even quiet parks. One afternoon last week, he saw a woman with dark hair at a café and his whole body went rigid. He left his coffee untouched and walked home, shaking.

He tells me that music was his language, his way of making sense of the world. Now the world feels like a small, locked room with someone breathing on the other side of the door. He doesn’t believe she’ll hurt him physically—she never did—but the feeling of being watched, of being known by a stranger who won’t stop, has hollowed him out.

He is polite, measured, sometimes even laughs at his own expense. “I used to play for hundreds of people,” he says. “Now I jump at the sound of my own refrigerator.” He looks down at his hands, the calluses fading. He hasn’t written a song in three years.
